```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

cyRAVEN labels cells using rules you wrote before you looked at the data. Those
rules are a prediction, and predictions can be wrong. Every check on this page
exists to find out whether yours was.

Work through them in this order. The first two catch most problems.

If you only have five minutes: open the two gate figures, check `staining_qc.csv`
for excluded samples, and look at the `source` column of `thresholds_used.csv`.
Anything that survives those three is probably worth believing.

## Look at the gates before the numbers

`recon_diagnostics.png` and `gating_qc.png` are drawn on every run and are the
only two figures you should read before anything else. They show, per sample,
where the scatter gate landed, where the singlet band sat, and where each marker
threshold ended up on the density it was derived from.

If a threshold sits on a shoulder instead of in a valley, you can see it here in
a second. No table will tell you as quickly.

## Did any sample fail staining?

`staining_qc.csv` gives a verdict per sample. A sample with no separable CD45
positive mode has nothing usable in it, and cyRAVEN excludes it and says so
rather than letting an unstained tube contribute a frequency of zero to your
group mean. Controls are recognised through the `is_control` column of the sample
map and are excluded from testing without being called failures.

`--include-qc-failed` overrides the exclusion when you want to look at what
happened.

## Does the phenotype match the label?

`population_marker_heatmap.png` puts markers in rows and your populations in
columns, z-scored across the run.

In a clustering-first workflow this figure names the clusters. Here it does the
opposite job: your populations already have names, so the figure is there to
contradict them. If the column labelled "CD4 T cells" does not show high CD4 and
low CD8, the gate is wrong, and you see it at a glance instead of inferring it
from a frequency that looked odd.

The figure outlines the cells your specification requires to be positive, reading
the same `populations:` block the scoring used, so the check cannot drift away
from the definitions it is checking.

`cohort_composition_heatmap.png` sits next to it and normalises every group to
the same notional cell count before splitting by population, so unequal sample
numbers and acquisition depth cannot produce the pattern on their own.

## Did the definition itself shift between groups?

This is the check most worth understanding, and no clustering-based tool has an
equivalent.

Because each sample gets its own cut-off, there is a trap. Suppose the patient
samples consistently need a lower CD4 cut-off than the controls. Then when you
compare "CD4 T cells" between the two groups, you are not comparing the same
thing in both. Part of any difference you find is a difference in where the line
was drawn, not in how many cells the patients have.

`threshold_drift_stats.csv` tests, for each protein, whether its cut-offs differ
systematically between your groups, and flags the ones that do. If a protein is
flagged, treat every cell type defined with it carefully: the gate is not
constant across the comparison.

## Does an independent grouping agree with you?

Switch this on with `--cluster`. cyRAVEN groups the cells purely by how similar
their protein levels are, never consulting your definitions, then compares the
two answers. Four patterns come out of it.

**A cluster that is mostly one of your labels.** Your definition and the data
agree. This is the outcome you want.

**A cluster whose cells are mostly labelled "other".** A real population exists
that your list does not describe. Rules alone can never find this, because you
cannot write a rule for something you have not thought of.

**One of your labels spread across several clusters.** Your definition is coarser
than the biology. The cells you are calling one type are at least two, and if
those subtypes move in opposite directions between groups, the overall frequency
will show nothing.

**A label with far fewer cells than the cluster it sits in.** Your cut-off is in
the wrong place. Say CD4 T cells come out at 0.3%, which would be almost none,
while a cluster holding 20% of all cells is clearly CD4 bright and labelled
"other". The cells are plainly there and the rule is rejecting them. Nothing in a
frequency table could tell you this.

Both readings are written to `cluster_gate_agreement_clusters.csv` and
`cluster_gate_agreement_populations.csv`.

## What was that undescribed cluster?

Being told that cluster 7 matches nothing you named is not much use on its own.
You cannot go back to the cytometer with a cluster number.

`--explain-clusters` closes that gap. For each unrecognised cluster, cyRAVEN
works out a short sequence of two-protein plots that would select those cells,
which is exactly the form a person would use to draw the gate by hand. You could
take the result to the instrument and reproduce it.

The gates it proposes are polygons rather than rectangles, and that matters
biologically. Real boundaries are often diagonal: CD4 against CD8 separates two T
cell lineages along a slanted line, not a square corner. Forcing a rectangle onto
a diagonal boundary either lets in cells that do not belong or throws away cells
that do.

Every score is measured on cells the fitting never saw, with the fitted score
printed next to it. A flexible shape can memorise a few thousand cells, so a
score measured on the same cells used to draw it will always look good. The gap
between the two numbers tells you whether it is real.

One caution. These are suggestions, not findings. A proposed gate says where some
cells sit, not that they are a meaningful cell type, and it comes with no
p-value. Nothing it produces feeds back into your frequencies or tests, which are
identical whether you run it or not.

Outputs: `cluster_gate_proposals.csv`, `cluster_gate_polygons.csv`, and one
`cluster_gate_strategy_<k>.png` per cluster.

## Is the difference really about age or sex?

If your patients are children and your controls are adults, any immune difference
you find could be a difference in age.

Two things have to be true at once before a variable is a genuine problem: it has
to differ between your groups, and it has to be related to the thing you are
measuring. Age differing between groups is harmless if age has no bearing on the
population you care about. So `confounding_diagnostics.csv` reports both facts
and gives a plain verdict in a `confounder_risk` column.

Statistically adjusting for age is a separate, opt-in step, and deliberately so.
With eight patients and eight controls, a model that also has to estimate age and
sex effects has very little information left for the comparison you actually
want. Worse, if nearly all your patients are young and nearly all your controls
are old, no amount of data can separate the two, because you have no young
controls to learn from. The adjusted number that comes out is a guess dressed up
with a confidence interval.

`--rank-ancova` will fit the adjusted model where there is enough data, and
labels every row `EXPLORATORY`. Where there is not, it writes `NOT FITTED` and
the reason, rather than a number that would sit in the folder looking as solid as
the others.

## Is there a batch effect, and is it safe to remove?

Samples processed on different days can differ for reasons that have nothing to
do with the people they came from. Point cyRAVEN at the column identifying the
processing day or run with `--batch-column`. If you do not, it uses the
acquisition date stored in the files, when that varies.

Two numbers come back, and you need both.

**Is there a batch effect at all?** `batch_mixing_stats.csv` asks whether cells
sit next to cells from their own batch more than they should. The raw score is
meaningless on its own, because how mixed cells can possibly get depends on how
many batches there are and how big each one is. So cyRAVEN shuffles the batch
labels at random and recomputes, which gives the score this dataset would produce
with no batch effect whatsoever. Your real score is compared against that.

**Would removing it also remove your finding?** `batch_group_confounding.csv`
measures how far batch membership and study group are the same thing. If every
patient was run on Tuesday and every control on Thursday, they are the same
thing, and there is no way to remove one without the other.

What happens next follows from those two. If the batches are separable from your
groups and the mixing is poor, `--correct-batch` lines up each protein's
distribution across batches. It does this in a way that cannot reorder cells
within a batch, so it can shift and stretch the values without inventing
structure that was not there.

If the two are too tangled, correction is refused and the run says why.
`--force-batch-correction` overrides it, and that decision is recorded in the run
manifest so anyone reading the results later can see it was made.

One thing worth knowing about what correction does and does not touch. It affects
the UMAP, the clustering, and the comparison between clusters and your gates. It
does not affect your population frequencies, the brightness measurements, or the
statistical tests, because those come from each sample's own cut-offs and are
already immune to batch. What a batch effect really distorts is the single map
built from all samples at once, and that is what gets fixed.

## Could someone else reproduce this run?

`run_manifest.txt` records the R version, the operating system, the version of
every software package actually loaded, which version of the code was used and
whether it had uncommitted edits, the exact command, and every setting in force.

As long as the results folder and its manifest stay together, you can always say
what produced the numbers, which is what a reviewer or a colleague picking the
project up in two years will ask.
